**Claude (Frontend Engineer · Visionary) — Round 1**

Looking at where this app actually stands: every upstream phase has converged hard on architecture principles (single CIFilter pipeline, one AuraStore, recipe/pixel determinism split, App Group for the widget), but nobody has yet fixed the actual seed-space — the mood/chip vocabulary and the concrete algorithm that turns (date, mood, chips) into a composition. That's been explicitly deferred twice (DEC-initial_discussion-007, [REDACTED:high_entropy]) and this is the phase that has to own it, because "data model" and "architecture" are meaningless without knowing what the seed space actually looks like.

I'll fix it here, decisively: 8 moods (Radiant, Calm, Wistful, Restless, Tender, Fierce, Hazy, Hopeful — chosen as a radial wheel so palette mapping has a coherent hue-rotation logic, not an arbitrary list), and 24 chips the user picks 1-2 of (word+emoji pairs grouped into four flavor families — texture, weather, pace, company — six each, so chip combinations carry semantic structure instead of being a flat grab-bag). That's 8 × (24 + C(24,2)) = 8 × 300 = 2,400 mood/chip combinations before you even factor in the date hash, which is plenty to make "different days feel meaningfully different" true by construction rather than by hope.

The algorithm itself: hash `dateKey|moodID|sortedChipIDs|timeOfDayBucket|entitlementTier|regenerationNonce` through SHA256, feed the digest into a splitmix64 PRNG, and draw the recipe fields off that stream in a fixed order (palette index, flow-field seed points, warp angle bias, particle/line density, color-grade curve, caption fragment indices). Here's the part I want to push hard on, because it's the actual make-or-break for "beautiful and varied, not a template recolored": don't build this as N fixed shape-field *templates* that get recolored per seed. Build a small deterministic simplex/value-noise implementation in pure Swift (maybe 80 lines, no dependency needed — this is well-trodden math) that generates a genuinely continuous flow-field from the seed, then drive `CIWarpKernel`/`CIColorKernel` control points off sampled noise values. That's the difference between "8 moods × a few palettes, obviously templated" and a composition space that's actually continuous and never repeats structurally. My honest risk callout on my own proposal: this is more implementation work than picking-from-a-list, and if the noise implementation is buggy it could produce ugly or degenerate output (e.g. banding, or fields that collapse to near-identical shapes for adjacent seeds) — so I'd want the debug render harness (already mandated by ios_architecture_review) to specifically include a handful of *adjacent* seeds (same mood, consecutive dates) in its canonical set, not just diverse ones, to catch exactly that failure mode before it ships.

Captions get the same combinatorial treatment rather than one flat curated list, both for variety and to solve a real edge case nobody's addressed: the 30-day no-repeat window ([REDACTED:high_entropy]) has to survive a user picking the same mood every day *and* regenerating every day — that's up to 60 draws against one mood's pool in 30 days. A flat "60+ hand-written phrases per mood × 8 moods" bank is a lot of curation to keep fresh. Instead: compose each caption from three independently-tracked fragment pools (opener / mood-core / chip-inflected closer, dozen-ish entries each), each with its own no-repeat window, selected deterministically from the same seed stream. Combinatorially that's thousands of effective captions from modest curation, and exhaustion becomes structurally near-impossible instead of something to hand-wave about.

On the client architecture side, I want to push one structural change beyond what design_handoff/ios_architecture_review specified: pull `Models` (recipe struct, DayEntry/MonthlyWrapped schema), `Engine` (seed hash, noise, palette/caption selection — pure Swift, zero UIKit/SwiftUI/CoreImage import), and `Persistence` (VersionedSchema, ModelContainer factory) into a local Swift Package, `AuraKit`, embedded via a local file:// package reference — not a third-party dependency, just proper module boundaries. Reasoning: the widget extension needs to decode `CachedCardMetadata` and the test target needs the engine with zero GPU/UIKit linkage (per the recipe/pixel determinism split), and a local package is the only way to guarantee the app target, widget target, and test target all link the *same* compiled code instead of three copies of a `.swift` file added to multiple targets that can silently drift. This is exactly the two-sources-of-truth failure shape this project has flagged repeatedly elsewhere — I'd rather kill it at the module-boundary level than rely on discipline.

Layout: `AuraKit/Sources/AuraKit/{Models,Engine,Persistence}`, `AuraKit/Tests/AuraKitTests` for the GPU-free determinism suite. Then the app target: `Aura/App` (entry point, scene), `Aura/Store` (AuraStore, PendingDeepLink), `Aura/Rendering` (CIContext-owning renderer, imports AuraKit's recipe types, produces bloom intermediates/thumbnail/export/Wrapped poster — this stays in the app target since it needs CoreImage+UIKit, not the pure-Swift package), `Aura/Services` (ClockProvider, DayStateService, StoreKitManager, NotificationScheduler, WidgetReloadCoordinator, ExportPipeline), `Aura/UI/{Theme,Components,Today,Archive,Wrapped,Settings}`, `Aura/DebugHarness` (compiled out via `#if DEBUG`). `AuraWidget/` extension target links AuraKit only for `CachedCardMetadata` decoding. `Shared/AppGroupConstants.swift` (App Group identifier, shared container URL helper) lives in AuraKit too since both targets need it.

One more architectural point I think is underspecified: date/timezone handling needs to be injectable, not just "verified by changing the Simulator's clock." I'm adding an `AuraClock` protocol (`now() -> Date`, `currentTimeZone() -> TimeZone`) that `AuraStore` and `DayStateResolver` take as a dependency, with `SystemClock` live and a `TestClock` for XCTest. This lets the DST/backward-clock/date-line edge cases (already decided) get fast, deterministic, CI-runnable unit tests instead of only being provable by a human manually flipping the Simulator's date — that manual pass stays as the acceptance-level check per the decision log, but it shouldn't be the *only* check on something this bug-prone.

Persistence: `ModelContainer` for the main store stays in the app's default private container (not the App Group) — only the rendered PNGs + `CachedCardMetadata` get written into the App Group shared container for the widget, per design_handoff. `SchemaV1` defines `DayEntry` (id = canonical date-string, mood, chipIDs, recipe as embedded Codable blob, image paths for full-res/thumbnail/4 bloom intermediates, captionText, isDemo, regenerationNonce, entitlementSnapshot, timeZoneIdentifierAtCompletion, createdAt) and `MonthlyWrapped` (monthKey, posterImagePath, dominantPaletteIndex, moodDistribution). `SchemaMigrationPlan` starts at v1 with an empty migration stage list, ready to extend.

Testing strategy: AuraKit unit tests cover recipe-struct determinism (same inputs → identical struct, hundreds of combos in milliseconds since there's no GPU), the noise/palette/caption selection logic, and `DayStateResolver` behavior under `TestClock`-injected DST transitions, backward clock moves, and date-line jumps. `StoreKitTest`/`SKTestSession` covers purchase/restore/refund/entitlement-listener flows in a normal XCTest target. The debug render harness (app-target only, `#if DEBUG`) batch-renders the canonical combination set — including adjacent-seed pairs per my noise-field concern above — plus the demo-vs-fresh parity set. Migration tests exercise `SchemaMigrationPlan` even at v1 to prove the harness itself works before it's ever needed for real.

**Coordinator (Claude) — decision after round 1**

Round 1 of tech_specs ran as another Claude solo pass — Codex is still in cooldown — but it did the one thing this phase actually needed: it stopped deferring the seed-space and fixed it. Two prior phases had explicitly punted "how many moods/chips, what's the actual algorithm" to this phase, and round 1 closed that decisively: 8 moods arranged as a radial wheel (so palette hue-mapping has real structure), 24 chips across four families of six (texture/weather/pace/company), user picks 1-2. That's 2,400 mood/chip combinations before the date even enters the hash. More importantly, it committed to a real algorithm rather than a lookup table: hash the composite key through SHA256 into a splitmix64 stream, and drive the actual composition off a small deterministic noise implementation (pure Swift, no dependency) rather than recoloring a fixed set of templates — which is the difference between "meaningfully different days" being true by construction versus true by hope. Captions get the same treatment: three independently-tracked fragment pools instead of one flat bank, so the 30-day no-repeat window survives even a user who regenerates daily against the same mood.

On architecture, the load-bearing call is pulling Models/Engine/Persistence into a local Swift Package (`AuraKit`) linked identically by the app target, the widget extension, and the test target — closing off the exact "three copies of a .swift file silently drift" failure mode this project has flagged repeatedly elsewhere, and giving the recipe/pixel determinism split (from ios_architecture_review) a real GPU-free test target to live in. An injectable `AuraClock` protocol (`SystemClock`/`TestClock`) was also added so the DST/backward-clock/date-line rules can get fast CI-runnable unit tests instead of relying solely on a human flipping the Simulator's date. A full `interfaces-json` contract came out of this round too, covering the recipe struct, persistence models, the renderer protocol, the store, StoreKit, widget metadata, and more.

What's still missing, and this is the actual Red Team catch the phase rules ask for: nothing in round 1 gives a *structural guarantee* that regeneration satisfies the already-locked acceptance bar (differ in ≥2 of palette/topology/density, [REDACTED:high_entropy]) — feeding a different nonce into the same hash makes divergence *likely* but not *guaranteed*, and a hash collision-adjacent case producing a regenerate that only shifts one field would be a real, testable bug that ships invisibly. Two smaller gaps: the mood-distribution trend view is explicitly required by the prompt and already scored should-have (DEC-app_features-004), but no data-aggregation interface for Swift Charts was specified this round; and the demo-history fixed-anchor date range ([REDACTED:high_entropy]) is still prose intent, not a concrete function signature. `PaletteTier` is referenced in `EntitlementSnapshot` but never defined.

CONSENSUS: NO

Next round needs to: (1) specify a concrete mechanism that structurally guarantees regeneration diverges in ≥2 of {palette, topology, density} — e.g. deriving those three fields from independent, well-separated lanes of the hash stream so a nonce change provably perturbs at least two of them, not just probabilistically — rather than leaving it to hash luck; (2) add the mood-distribution/trend aggregation interface for Swift Charts; (3) add a concrete `DemoHistoryAnchor`-style function for the fixed pre-real-usage date range; (4) define `PaletteTier` and how the Aura+ "expanded palette library" unlock actually maps onto the palette index space.

Right, the coordinator's catch is real and I want to own it fully rather than patch around it — "probably diverges" is not the same claim as "differs in ≥2 of palette/topology/density," and [REDACTED:high_entropy] was explicit that this needs to be a testable acceptance bar, not a hope. Feeding a different nonce into one shared SHA256→splitmix64 stream and drawing sequential fields off it means every field's divergence probability is bounded by its own domain size — if paletteIndex is `hash mod 16`, there's a real 1-in-16 chance two adjacent nonces land on the same palette, and if that coincides with a density collision too (also plausible at small deltas), you've shipped a regenerate button that silently does nothing for a real user on a bad-luck day. That's not a hypothetical edge case, it's a statistically guaranteed occurrence at scale given how many regenerations will happen across the install base.

So I want to flip this from probabilistic to algebraic. Compute the base recipe (nonce=0) normally off the hash stream, then for any nonce>0, run it through a `RegenerationDivergenceEngine` that *forces* structural displacement rather than re-drawing and hoping: paletteIndex_new = `(paletteIndex_base + 1 + (nonceHash mod (paletteCount - 1))) mod paletteCount` — that's a nonzero offset mod count, which mathematically cannot equal the base value, full stop, no probability involved. Same trick for the flow-field seed (XOR with a nonce-derived nonzero mask, guaranteed ≠ base) and for density (force a minimum absolute delta in a hash-chosen direction, clamped/wrapped at the domain edges so it can't get stuck at a boundary). That gives you a *provable* ≥2-of-3 divergence — really 3-of-3 with margin — and it's the kind of thing you can write as one deterministic unit test that never flakes: generate 500 (mood, chips, date) triples, assert regenerate always differs in at least 2 fields, done, no statistical assertions, no "run it enough times and hope."

And since I'm already in there forcing divergence, I want to push the visual stakes higher than just numeric field differences — this is where I'll go full Visionary on the group. The prompt itself names three composition families: "painterly gradient blooms, particle fields, or flow-field line art." Right now our recipe treats that as one continuous noise-driven engine with palette/density/topology params, which is good for the *daily* variety story, but it means a regeneration could still look like "the same kind of picture, shifted a bit" even with the forced numeric divergence — technically compliant, but not what the app promised ("regenerate once per day if unsatisfied" implies the user gets something that reads as a real alternative, not a nudge). So I want to add `CompositionFamily` as a first-class field in `AuraRecipe` — `paintBloom` / `particleField` / `flowLines`, drawn from its own hash lane for the base card, and on regeneration *forced* to a different family via the same nonzero-offset trick. That means a paid regeneration doesn't just get a new palette, it can genuinely switch from a soft gradient bloom to a particle field — which is a much stronger fulfillment of "make the purchase's emotional promise real" than shifting a density slider. Yes, this means `AuraRenderer` needs three composition-strategy branches instead of one filter graph with parameterized topology — more surface area to build and to keep visually consistent with each other in quality — but I don't think that's scope creep, I think it's literally what the prompt asked for by naming three distinct visual languages instead of one. If we ship only one continuous noise field forever, "particle fields" and "flow-field line art" from the original prompt never actually happen, and that's a real gap between what was promised and what gets built.

On the palette/PaletteTier gap: I'll define the library as 32 total curated palettes, free tier drawing from the first 16 (`paletteIndex mod 16`), Aura+ drawing from the full 32 (`paletteIndex mod 32`) — so the "expanded palette library" unlock isn't a separate settings toggle, it's literally a wider modulus applied at generation time using the already-snapshotted `EntitlementSnapshot`, which keeps it fully consistent with [REDACTED:high_entropy] (past cards never retroactively change just because entitlement changed later). `PaletteLibrary.paletteCount(for:)` returns 16 or 32, `PaletteLibrary.resolvePalette(index:tier:)` does the lookup.

For demo history, "fixed range strictly before real usage" needs to be frozen once and never recomputed, or you get drift if someone toggles demo on, waits a week, toggles it off, toggles it back on. So: compute the anchor exactly once, the first time demo mode is ever enabled, as `anchorEnd = (earliest real DayEntry's date ?? today) - 1 day`, `anchorStart = anchorEnd - 33 days` (34 days total — comfortably past the 30+ requirement so the trend chart and Wrapped-preview have real breathing room), persist that computed range, and every subsequent demo-history render reads the persisted range rather than recomputing from "now." That structurally makes date collision with real usage impossible even years later, not just impossible today.

And for the trend view — I'll make it genuinely chart-ready rather than a vague "aggregation function": `MoodTrendAggregator.chartData(entries:range:granularity:)` returns `[MoodTrendDataPoint]` where each point is `(bucketDate, mood, count)` — that's a direct `Chart { BarMark(x: .value("Week", bucketDate), y: .value("Count", count)).foregroundStyle(by: .value("Mood", mood)) }` with weekly buckets as the default granularity for a 30-ish day window. Demo-labeled entries participate in the aggregate the same way they do in the archive grid — the point of demo mode is a non-empty trend view on first review, and the archive's existing demo-badge/banner treatment already covers the "don't silently pass this off as real" requirement, so the chart doesn't need its own separate demo-exclusion logic, just needs to read from the same `isDemo`-flagged entries.

I think this closes everything the coordinator flagged, plus raises the actual ceiling on what "genuinely beautiful and varied" means by making family-switching a real mechanism instead of leaving it implicit in prose. The one new risk I'm introducing and want on the record: three composition-family filter graphs is meaningfully more rendering code than one parameterized noise field, and if the team only has bandwidth to build one well, I'd rather we build one family excellently than three families mediocrely — so if this gets cut under time pressure, my strong preference is cut it down to two families (bloom + one of particle/flow-line) rather than force all three through at lower quality, since a mediocre third family actively hurts the "beauty is the single most important requirement" bar more than not having it at all.
